#2806. NFL didn't know Puka Nacua had surgery when agreeing to suspension

The sudden decision of the NFL to suspend receiver Puka Nacua three games raises plenty of relevant questions. On Friday, a technically irrelevant question was answered.

After Rams coach Sean McVay disclosed to reporters that Nacua had surgery to repair a torn MCL suffered during a Week 9 win over the Commanders, Judy Battista of NFL Network reported this: “The NFL did not know Puka Nacua had had knee surgery on Tuesday when it suspended him yesterday.”

Surely, that’s accurate; Judy is a solid reporter. But that extra fact doesn’t matter to the NFL’s ultimate handling of Nacua.

The report creates the impression that, during the negotiations that resulted in the three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua and/or his representatives withheld material information. That, at some level, the league had been duped by the lack of knowledge that Nacua had undergone surgery that will sideline him for “a couple months.”

First, the suspension (as the league affirmatively explained on Thursday) is separate from the injury. The NFL listed multiple examples of players who served suspensions while injured.

Second, whether Nacua (who had already missed one of the four minimum games he’s required to miss while on IR), was already going to serve the entirety of the suspension while on injured reserve with or without surgery.

Third, the surgery and the extended absence actually avoids the possibility that Nacua would have returned to action exactly one game after finishing his suspension, resulting in no net games missed due to the suspension.

The mere existence of the report represents an implicit acknowledgement by the league that the negotiated suspension, aimed at allowing Nacua to double-dip when it comes to his stint on injured reserve and his suspension, underscores the broader question of whether players should be allowed to serve a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy when otherwise unable to play. That’s a separate issue for the NFL to revisit, if it chooses, through a potential revision to the terms of the policy.

As explained on Friday, the league could have refused the deal. It could have insisted on pushing the issue through the full process, with Judge Sue L. Robinson conducting a hearing and the outcome potentially being appealed (by Nacua and/or the league) to the Commissioner. But that would have entailed a non-zero-percent chance that Nacua wouldn’t have been suspended at all.

For Nacua, the goal was to get the suspension served while injured. The fact that he had surgery before the agreement was reached gave him more of a buffer than the NFL knew about, expanding the window during which the suspension could be fully served before the end of the 2026 season without Nacua missing time due to the suspension. Which would still allow Nacua to have this issue behind him before the 2027 offseason, when he signs a new contract with the Rams, has the franchise tag applied, or becomes a free agent.

Of course, Nacua now needs to tread lightly. The league has made it clear that “any further violation of the Personal Conduct Policy, including failing to satisfy the conditions of his diversion program, will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the League.” To the extent that the league isn’t thrilled by the perception/reality that it allowed Nacua to serve his suspension at a time when he otherwise could not play, the league could be ready to pounce on any opportunity to impose a longer suspension that would apply when Nacua is healthy again.

#2799. 3 biggest positions of need for Patriots to address in future

With the state of the New England Patriots' season in question following Drake Maye's injury, a way-too-early look ahead to the upcoming offseason in 2027 shines a light on three positions that stand out as priorities.

It shouldn't come as a surprise that two of those positions are on the defensive side of the ball. The Patriots entered the season with what was expected to be one of the best defensive units in the NFL. However, recent run-ins with more talented offenses has led to some second-guessing.

The Patriots aren't out of playoff contention, but they are also in a place where they'll be eyeing individual performances even more closely to see who stays and who goes in the offseason. This last stretch of football will be make or break for some players on the roster.

Here are the three biggest positions of need for the team in the offseason:

The Patriots have not gotten strong production from Dre'Mont Jones so far this season, as he has recorded only 1.5 sacks. Elijah Ponder needs to finish the year strong and prove that he is capable of being a reliable pass-rusher over the course of a full 17-game season, though what he has shown through 10 weeks of the year so far has been impressive.

Not only so, but Harold Landry has yet to return from the reserve/physically unable to perform list and is advancing in age, further necessitating a high-end edge rusher to join the team's ranks. Regardless of Ponder's development, New England needs another established presence off the edge.

Adding a high-end pass-rusher in free agency, such as Tuli Tuipulotu, or a championship-caliber performer in Uchenna Nwosu, is a move that the team could benefit from making.

Milton Williams and Christian Barmore give the Patriots a talented starting combination, but the team needs more depth behind the two. Williams has recorded two sacks and five tackles for loss this season, while Barmore has 4.5 sacks, nine tackles for loss and a forced fumble on the year.

Adding a high-quality interior defender such as free agent Kobie Turner might be a smart move for the team to make. New England also needs a high-end third option such as free agent Roy Robertson-Harris, who is capable of potentially stepping into a starting role if the organization decides to trade Barmore in the offseason.

The Patriots have room to add another high-end receiver to complement their existing group. Finding a legitimate third option will give the offense another dynamic weapon and help take pressure off of Drake Maye. If New England's season continues to unravel with Maye sidelined by an ankle injury, the team will stand to gain from having a higher draft selection to use on an elite wide receiver prospect, the likes of Charlie Becker or Nick Marsh.

The open market will also present the Patriots with an opportunity to acquire an established veteran who is capable of contributing immediately next to A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs, the likes of Parker Washington and Rashee Rice in free agency.

#2798. Will Shane Steichen be back in 2027?

After the 2025 season ended, Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon put both G.M. Chris Ballard and coach Shane Steichen on notice that much was expected in 2026.

Then, one day after the Colts lost to the Titans in Week 6, she fired Ballard and kept Steichen.

Nearly five weeks later, Steichen remains. After next Sunday’s game against the Giants, the Colts will enter their bye. That’s typically the best time for an in-season coaching change, since it gives the interim coach maximum time to get up to speed before the next game.

Creating a vacancy with six weeks left in the regular season carries a separate benefit. The team can get a head start on searching for the replacement. And if ownership already knows the coach will be fired after the season ends, it makes no sense to delay that part of the process.

So here’s the question. Will Irsay-Gordon bring Steichen back in 2027?

It makes no sense to keep a new G.M. from hiring a new coach. Every G.M. arrives with a wish list of coaches who would be pursued, if/when the position is vacant. It makes plenty of sense to give a new G.M. an immediate vacancy to fill.

But what about the Colts this year has made sense? The firing of the G.M. left the team without a seasoned, experienced executive to navigate the strategy of making, or not making, trades. They quickly moved guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner. They rejected offers for running back Jonathan Taylor and quarterback Daniel Jones. They moved two starting receivers — Keenan Allen and Josh Downs — on the day of the trade deadline.

Steichen has been operating for much of the season with one hand tied behind his back. Now, he’ll have both wrists secured. Whatever the decision will be as to Steichen, it’s unfair to base it on the team’s overall performance since the Nelson and Buckner trades.

Before that point, they took the Chiefs to overtime in Kansas City. They beat the Texans. They manhandled the Commanders in London. They took the Vikings to the limit in Minnesota.

Although the signs point to Steichen eventually being fired, the fact that he’s still there now means he could still be there later. The new G.M. may be expected to work with him.

It’s ultimately the owner’s call. And the owner may have strong feelings about Steichen’s skills and abilities, based on the fact that she’s on the sideline every week.

If she was upstairs, she’d likely be hearing criticism of the head coach during the game. Instead, she’s watching him in his element. And she hasn’t fired him yet.

Throw in the fact that a new coach may not be as welcoming to the owner’s presence in the bench area, and she may be even more inclined to give Steichen (who’s fine with it) another chance. Especially since she systematically began making his job much more difficult the moment the Colts traded Nelson and Buckner.

Moving forward, it’ll be virtually impossible. The fact that Steichen has survived this long could mean that he’ll survive whatever comes next.

#2797. Wembanyama scores 50 as Spurs crush Pelicans to close homestand

The San Antonio Spurs closed out their three-game homestand with a 114-91 victory over the New Orleans Pelicans at the Frost Bank Center on Saturday night in front of a sold out crowd, which included one very special celebrity guest, singer and actress Selena Gomez.

Victor Wembanyama posted 50 points, 18 rebounds, 5 three-pointers, and 5 blocks in 32 minutes. At one point during the first half, Wembanyama hit one of his five threes on the night, turned towards the crowd and smiled in Gomez's direction.

"I had to show off for Selena (Gomez)," he said, smiling as he answered.

Wembanyama came out aggressive from the opening tip, scoring 17 of the Spurs' 32 points in the opening quarter. He went to rim for dunks, hit free throws, and scored from the mid range. San Antonio had 30 assists on the night and 14 of those were off a made Wemby basket. Nothing New Orleans did worked on this night to stop the Spurs' French star from accomplishing his goal of scoring 50 points, no matter how hard they tried.

Pelicans coach Jamahl Mosley doubled Wembanyama with multiple players, but the Spurs' forward backed down the smaller player right into the paint or when he was triple teamed, he found Julian Champagnie or Devin Vassell for an open three.

"I thought he started the game off aggressive," Spurs Head Coach Mitch Johnson said of Wembanyama after the game. "It's so interesting when people play like that, especially with his talent and then it helps with your shots. I thought he did a really good job of playing with force."

Despite Wembanyama's great night, Johnson still had a criticism for his star player and that is his passing. Late in the half, Wemby secured a defensive rebound and brought the ball up court. Instead of finding the open Keldon Johnson, the French star pulled up for three and missed, ignoring his open teammate.

"Keldon has to have the ball in that moment," Mitch Johnson said. "When you play the right way, things like that happen."

As good as the Spurs looked on Saturday, they still struggled in the non-Wemby minutes. New Orleans outscored the Spurs 22-13 in the first half when Wembanyama sat, but things were even when he sat in the second half. The reason? Johnson put in Luke Kornet, Harrison Barnes, and Carter Bryant. However, he kept Devin Vassell and Stephon Castle on the floor with that second unit.

"I thought we had some moments where we did a really good job defensively in terms of shrinking the floor and showing crowds and gang rebounding," Mitch Johnson said. "That group, probably, the worst minutes of the non Victor, has nothing to do with Luke, in my opinion. It's when we take quick shots, and then we're in transition defense a lot, and we're on our heels."

As a result of those lineup changes, Castle turned it on and scored 19 points on the night to go along with six assists.

"It's been reflective ever since he's been on this team," Wembanayama said of Castle. "He's been impactful in a meaningful way and he's impacted winning ever since he arrived here."

Keldon Johnson had 10 points off the bench, scoring in double figures for the fourth time in the last five games. If he can continue to deliver at that level consistently, the bench unit will be much improved as the season goes on. "When I do the right things on the court, the scoring will come," Keldon said after the game.

De'Aaron Fox slipped on a wet spot on the floor during the first half and was limping a bit before being taken out of the game. He would return later and Mitch Johnson said after the game that Fox was fine. Still, Fox scored just 5 points on 1-for-4 shooting and one has to wonder if his hip injury is bothering him.

The Spurs are now 14-3 on the season and will return to the court on Monday night when they face the Sacramento Kings at 9 p.m.

#2796. Raiders owner Mark Davis hated the Madden movie

The new Madden movie includes a brief, fleeting glance of a young Mark Davis. The depiction wasn’t flattering.

His assessment of the film is far less flattering.

The Raiders owner teed off on the Madden movie, in an interview with John Katsolimetes of the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

“My comment is, it’s full of turducken,” Davis said initially.

“It depends on whether you like turducken or not, and obviously, I don’t like turducken,” Davis said.

“I think it’s really it’s unfair to take people that have passed away and make caricatures out of them, and try to sell it as truth,” Davis said. “They start the movie with a statement saying that all of it’s not true, but some of it is, so it’s confusing what to believe.”

That’s not an uncommon device. “Based on a true story” means that plenty of liberties will be taken in an effort to make the story more compelling.

Mark Davis had one specific concern regarding the shading of the truth. He objected to his father’s reaction to the serious neck injury suffered by Patriots receiver Darryl Stingley, during a preseason game in 1978.

“So John goes over to the hospital afterwards, you know, and really looks after him,” Mark Davis said, “and there’s a scene where my dad is telling John, ‘You don’t need to go over there. You don’t need to take care of other teams’ players. You take care of our players.’

“That’s just so far from the truth. Anybody who has ever known him knows my dad always took care of people behind the scenes. If it was a player from another team had an issue that wasn’t being taken care of, my dad would quietly take care of that even if it was players on other teams. I’m serious. . . . It just it felt cheap to me to build up John’s image at the expense of my father’s.”

Davis praised Christian Bale for his portrayal of Al Davis.

“You can’t blame the script on him,” Mark Davis said. “He tried.”

Mark Davis also didn’t care for the characterization of the iconic John Madden by Nicolas Cage.

“You know, he at times did look like John, but he wasn’t John,” Davis said. “I mean, they made John to be a pussy, and John was the farthest thing from a pussy.”

The end result could be a positive. Mark Davis is now motivated to create something that properly and accurately depicts his father.

“I don’t know what this movie’s purpose was, to be honest,” Mark Davis said. “But you know, it’s making me more and more realize that I’m going to have to put together something on my dad. It could be a movie, it could be a characterization, but at least it’ll be truthful. . . .

“I think I need to do that, or at least let people know that I’m thinking about doing that, so that don’t jump in and think that they can do it first.”

The concerns expressed by Mark Davis regarding the script raise the question of whether he or the league or anyone bothered to review it before allowing the producers to use the Raiders name, colors, and logos in the filming of the football sequences. That’s a critical aspect when it comes to the overall credibility of a film about pro football.

If it looks real, it feels real. Unlike other films that didn’t secure the ability to use actual team names and logos (Any Given Sunday, The Replacements).

And that’s the irony of this. Davis and the league allowed the Raiders name and uniforms to be included in the film, giving it the impression of accuracy and authenticity. Which, in turn, makes the story seem accurate and authentic. Which makes it even harder to separate the truth from the fiction.

Here’s hoping Mark Davis comes up with a way to tell the true story of Al Davis. With no embellishment, fabrication, or Hollywood tricks aimed at making the story seem better than it was.

Because the story of Al Davis would be pretty damn compelling if it were indeed confined to the strict parameters of reality.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2789. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

#2779. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2778. Has Rasul Douglas been Adam Peters’ best off season addition?

Following an extended time period on injured reserve for 2025 second-round pick Trey Amos, the Washington Commanders added Rasul Douglas late in free agency, signing the veteran just before the start of training camp in July. At the time, there were multiple questions surrounding the addition of a soon-to-be 31-year-old cornerback for a team that desperately needed playmakers in the secondary.

Douglas worked behind fellow cornerbacks Mike Sainristil and Amik Robertson to start the season, and while he only played 38% of the team's total defensive snaps in Week 1, Rasul immediately made a mark with his physical play style.

Eventually, Douglas would take over a full-time role for the Commanders' defense in Week 4, logging 85% of the total defensive snaps and recording 5 tackles, 1 assist, 2 stops, 1 interception, and 1 pass defended versus the Colts. Post-game, Rasul proved his fit for Washington's competitive culture, stating the secondary's improved performance was not good enough, as the team didn't win the matchup. The following week, Douglas backed his words with his own play, finishing second on the team with 9 tackles and 1 assist while being graded with 4 receptions for 39 receiving yards allowed on 9 targets by Pro Football Reference.

Trey Amos returned to the lineup in Week 6, and while his return, along with the addition of safety Nick Cross, has been attributed to the improvement of the Commanders' secondary, Douglas' performance as a third cornerback cannot be overlooked. Since Week 6 in San Francisco, Washington's defense has given up just 18.5 points per game and the secondary has not allowed more than one passing touchdown in each of those contests. While that stretch did include games against the struggling Eagles and last week's road trip to New York, it also included games against the 49ers and Rams. Through Week 10, per @SFdata9ers, Douglas has a league-low 39.6 allowed passer rating while also leading the team in interceptions with 3, including a game-sealing grab at Metlife Stadium.

Identified in the off-season as a potential fit for Daronte Jones' defensive scheme, in addition to being a ball-hawk, Douglas has been a sure tackler, recording 29 total tackles (22 solo) on the season and 7 passes defended; just 2 behind full-time starter Amik Robertson. With Robertson's availability in question for Monday night's matchup against the Cincinnati Bengals' elite passing offense, Douglas may be called on to prove his value yet again, but fans may take comfort in the fact the Commanders' cornerback ranks 9th on Pro Football Network's cornerback grading list headed into Week 11.

What is the best part of Rasul Douglas' performance thus far?

He was signed to a 1-year, $1.8 million agreement with only $580k of guaranteed money and up to $2 million available in incentives. Those numbers rank him 95th on Spotrac's average cornerback contract rankings, yet halfway through the season, Douglas is playing at a top ten level. That makes the free agent addition arguably the best of Adam Peters' off season acquisitions so far and a player the Washington Commanders should consider keeping around next season.

#2777. The Nasdaq is in freefall. Here's one stock to look at

I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon.

Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

#2775. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. The project is supported by 20-year firm transportation agreements and is expected to enter service in 2030. ET expects to ultimately own 51% of the $1.6 billion project.

The 5-star analyst said that Energy Transfer lowered its 2026 capital spending outlook to $5.5 billion (midpoint of the guidance range) from $5.75 billion due to project timing. Energy Transfer expects capex to rise to $7 billion in 2027, while Gabelman projects $5 billion in both 2028 and 2029, based on disclosed projects.

Gabelman also highlighted management's commentary about optimization initiatives contributing an incremental $800 million to 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a larger benefit than in recent years. "A return to less commodity volatility should the [Middle East] war end could bring some relative downside, though this is offset by continued strong growth prospects," he said.

#2773. ‘It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround

'It worked every time': How Sixers found a clutch answer at shootaround originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers created their two cleanest late-game looks several hours before they needed them.

During Wednesday morning's shootaround in Orlando, Nick Nurse had the Sixers work on offensive material they had not consistently used this season. They tested one of those actions during the first half, returned to it throughout the closing minutes and watched it produce the shots they needed to complete a 17-point comeback.

"We worked on some stuff this morning that we hadn't used before, and they ran all that stuff very, very well and very calmly and with composure," Nurse told reporters.

The Sixers have earned six of their 13 wins after trailing by double digits. They are also 11-0 in games that reached clutch time.

Relying on comebacks is not a sustainable plan. The repeated late-game situations, however, have forced a new roster to respond to different lineups, coverages and responsibilities while the season is still young.

Each close finish gives Nurse more information about which players and actions hold up when possessions tighten. Wednesday gave him a new option.

Anfernee Simons' clinching three in the Sixers' 121-116 win over the Magic was the final result of that preparation.

"That last play, we ran that play in the first half," Simons said. "We worked it a couple of times, and in the second half we ran that play every single time down the stretch, and it worked every time.

"It was a play we ran through. [It's gratifying] especially when it's working consistently and you're getting different shots out of it and the opposing team just don't know what to do.

"We just continue to run the play and get the open shots we need."

NBC Sports Philadelphia video producer and Sixers Talk podcast co-host Kevin Rice broke down how the Sixers used its different options to keep Orlando guessing.

The action begins with two players stationed near the elbows. A player on the opposite elbow then sets a screen for the player up top, who receives the ball while moving around it.

The Sixers ran the set three consecutive times during the first half. None of the possessions reached the primary option. Each still produced a quality opportunity.

On the first, Joel Embiid cleared LeBron James out of the area and directed Simons around him for a dribble handoff. Simons received an open three-point look.

Orlando took away the handoff the next time down but left Embiid one-on-one against Wendell Carter Jr. Embiid created enough room to retrieve his own miss and convert an and-one opportunity.

The third attempt pulled Orlando's defense into the paint. Two passes moved the ball through the collapsing coverage and created an open three for VJ Edgecombe.

"We had a little thing where he comes flying off behind Joel, and he doesn't get to do that that much, right?" Nurse said of Simons. "So tonight he gets the opportunity to do it, and it was very good for us on a number of plays."

The Sixers changed the action late without abandoning its initial Horns alignment. Simons moved through the lane to help form a Spain pick-and-roll involving James and Embiid.

On the first late possession, Simons remained near the play after James gained a matchup against Carter. Orlando struggled to sort out its assignments, leaving James open for a 19-foot jumper with 54.8 seconds remaining.

After Jalen Suggs made one of two free throws, the Sixers returned to the same setup. This time, Simons relocated to the left corner after James drew Carter on a switch.

James drove into the paint. Suggs lost track of Simons while responding to the penetration, and James sent the ball toward the corner.

Simons buried the open three to give the Sixers a 119-113 lead with 15 seconds left.

"Bron just penetrated the paint," Simons said. "It kind of got some confusion, and when I was on the dunker and kind of spaced out to the corner, I ended up finding myself wide open for the three, and Bron found me."

The Sixers entered the night without Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown, their two leading scorers. Simons made his first start with Philadelphia and recorded 18 points in the city where he grew up.

His final basket also illustrated why Nurse believes the Sixers have more to uncover with him.

"When he's out there, they gotta be really careful," Nurse said. "So I think there's some drives he creates, and just about every time he lets it go, whether he's on balance or not, you think it's going in, and that is a big deal. Like, that is a big deal.

"And again, I think we're still a ways away from really unlocking him to being even more part of some of the things we can do with him to create more shots."

Philadelphia is now 11-0 in clutch games. The finish in Orlando provided a more specific explanation than experience or shot-making alone.

The Sixers installed a set in the morning, explored its counters and trusted it when the game tightened. James supplied the patience to read Orlando's coverage. Embiid occupied the middle of the action. Simons moved without the ball, and Edgecombe remained ready to shoot.

James said his heart rate drops when close games increase the pressure on everyone else.

"I mean, experience," James said. "A guy that's seen every situation this league has to offer. It's nothing I haven't seen. And, you know, in the moments where people's heart rate goes up or anxiety goes up, mine is pretty low. It's actually lower, you know."

The Sixers still have more actions and reads to learn as Nurse becomes familiar with his new personnel, but their latest win showed their innate ability to adapt in big moments.

"I think we're still a long ways away from knowing all the reads and all that stuff because it's just a little early, right?" Nurse said.

#2772. Clemson 20, Duke 10: Position grades for the Blue Devils

Duke's defense did its part on Friday night, holding Clemson to 20 points, but the Blue Devils' offense failed to put much of anything together in the 20-10 loss.

The Tigers' defense focused on keeping Nate Sheppard in check, putting the pressure on Walker Eget and Duke's passing game. It worked out for Dabo Swinney's squad.

Here is how Duke's positions graded out in the loss.

Clemson's defense planned to make anyone but Nate Sheppard beat them, and it fell on Walker Eget's shoulders. The quarterback failed to take the opportunity, going 16-of-38 for 149 yards and an interception.

Nate Sheppard was bottled up for most of the game, with his one touchdown coming on a 55-yard run. Clemson made sure he wouldn't single-handedly beat them.

If it weren't for Javon Nicholas, this grade would be much lower, but he caught six passes for 87 yards. The rest of the wide receivers? Two catches for four total yards.

Jeremiah Hasley was his usual self, catching six passes for 55 yards.

Clemson brought pressure for much of the game, sacking Eget twice, but with the box loaded, the offensive line didn't have much chance to get Sheppard going.

No sacks, but as Manny Diaz explained, that was more to do with what Clemson was doing (quick passes and quarterback runs) than how the Duke defensive line played. Allowing 220 rush yards is never ideal, though.

Not being able to keep discipline on quarterback runs, plus not making a difference in the backfield, yields a bad grade.

They weren't challenged much, as Clemson attempted just 30 passes, completing 17 of them.

A missed field goal by Gavin Strange hurt the Blue Devils, but Kade Reynoldson averaged 43.8 yards per punt.

Diaz got outcoached by Dabo Swinney in every way.

#2771. NFL wife opens up on chaotic 24 hours after Chiefs cut returner ‘out of the blue’

While life in the NFL may seem glamorous, one NFL WAG is giving fans a peek at the chaos it can also entail in a post on social media.

Maureen Remigio, a former Philippine track and field star and the wife of NFL wide receiver and return specialist Nikko Remigio, shared the blow-by-blow of what it was like to learn that her husband had been cut by the Chiefs earlier this month.

Nikko Remigio had been Kansas City's starting punt returner for three years before the decision was made to cut him in order to make room for the newly acquired Josh Downs, whom the Chiefs picked up in a trade with the Colts on Nov. 10.

Maureen began spilling the tea — while drinking Chinese herbal tea in her video — about how Nikko had first became aware of the move when he received a text "out of the blue" from the Chiefs.

"We just got a text that he needs to come in, bring his iPad and that's it," she explained in her social media post. "Really just want to make you guys understand how quick everything happens."

With Nikko on waivers, he was free to be picked up by any NFL team that wanted to put a claim in on him, and Maureen explained the torture that goes into the 24-hour period when a player could be picked up by another team.

Houston Texans wide receiver Nikko Remigio returns a kick against Cleveland Browns wide receiver Malachi Corley on Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, in Cleveland. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

"Within those 24 hours, you don't know where you're going," she said. "You don't know who's going to get you, if you're going to get claimed or not, and what your options are.

"So you can just imagine the waiting game, the sitting around, the walking around the house, the uncertainty that just happened in a snap of a finger. "Almost close to the 24th hour was when we found out that the Texans claimed Nikko."

Maureen Remigio at a Chiefs game mauemily/Instagram

But the chaos wasn't over just yet for the Remigios.

The Texans booked Nikko's flight out of Kansas City for a little more than two hours after he found out he was headed to Houston, meaning a mad scramble to get things together and get to the airport.

Maureen described just throwing clothes into his suitcase and rushing him to the airport, and "just like that, he's in Houston."

Nikko made his debut for the Texans in their loss to the Browns in Week 10, averaging 28.5 yards on kickoff returns and 14.5 yards on punt returns.

But Maureen's post was a glimpse into the side of a "very cold business sometimes."

"This is just the side of professional football that not a lot of people understand," she explained. "Like you can have a job yesterday and the next day you might not have a job. Not all athletes' contracts are guaranteed and Nikko, being an undrafted free agent, he has always had to fight for his spot on the roster, and now I'm just excited to be with him."

#2770. CeeDee Lamb fined $23,882 for block the league used as a highlight

When Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb made a downfield block on a George Pickens touchdown catch Sunday against the 49ers, the league’s website was so impressed that the highlight video on NFL.com emphasized Lamb’s block over Pickens’ touchdown.

“Can’t-Miss Play: CeeDee Lamb’s HUGE block springs Pickens free for 39-yard TD,” the caption on the highlight video says.

Calling the play on Fox, Tom Brady praised Lamb, immediately recognizing it as a great downfield block.

But the league’s disciplinary process didn’t think it was so great. Lamb has been fined $23,882 for what the NFL deemed “Unnecessary Roughness: Use of the helmet.”

Lamb confirmed to reporters on Thursday that he had been informed he was getting fined, but he insisted he didn’t make contact with his helmet and found it frustrating that receivers take hits routinely but get fined when they make one.

“I can block, and I’m real good at doing things like that, but I get fined,” Lamb said. “I never touched him with my helmet. . . . I guess as a receiver, we can get hit, but can’t deliver the punishment.”

Lamb will surely appeal the fine for what looked, both to the league’s website and the league’s all-time greatest player, like a good block.

#2769. Observations after Sixers survive Bucks' late surge, reach 14-3

Observations after Sixers survive Bucks' late surge, reach 14-3 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers survived the Bucks' late surge and reached 14-3 on the season Saturday afternoon with a 132-129 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

Tyler Herro nearly sent the game to overtime with a buzzer-beating three-pointer, but replays showed that he released his shot late.

Herro had a massive performance for the 1-16 Bucks, posting a career-high 50 points on 15-for-23 shooting, 11 rebounds and seven assists.

Joel Embiid had 26 points, a season-high 17 rebounds and nine assists for the Sixers.

LeBron James (21 points), Tyrese Maxey (17 points) and Anfernee Simons (18) were among the seven Sixers to score in double figures.

The Sixers were down Jaylen Brown (left hamstring strain), Dean Wade (left hamstring tightness/soreness), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

Next up for the Sixers is a Monday night meeting with the Trail Blazers. Here are observations on their victory over the Bucks:

Maxey returned to the Sixers' starting five after missing the team's comeback win Wednesday over the Magic with right foot soreness. He was joined by VJ Edgecombe, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, James and Embiid.

James threw down a dunk on the day's first play. Embiid then dished to a cutting Edgecombe for a layup that put the Sixers up 4-0.

The Bucks quickly found a foothold in the game.

Embiid missed his first four shots, including two that were swatted by Myles Turner. Maxey began 1 for 5 from the floor. Herro canned a three-pointer to give Milwaukee a 15-8 lead.

The Sixers entered the game with a minus-13.2 net rating in first quarters, which ranked 28th in the NBA. They faced a 30-29 deficit after Saturday's first period.

Even with Maxey available again, Labaron Philon Jr. deservingly stayed in the Sixers' rotation following an excellent outing in Orlando.

He scored two points in six first-half minutes. The 20-year-old made a rookie mistake at the tail end of the first quarter, fouling Herro on a three-point attempt.

Dominick Barlow checked in for his first action of the season with 2:51 remaining in the first quarter. He'd been sidelined for the Sixers' first 16 games because of a lower back stress reaction.

Barlow scored his first points early in the second quarter when he tipped in a Maxey miss. He then teamed up with James in crowd-pleasing style, sprinting ahead of the pack on a fast break and flushing home the 22-time All-Star's long-distance lob.

The afternoon was not devoid of rust for Barlow. Shortly after that alley-oop, he grabbed an offensive rebound, dribbled out to the perimeter and fired an open three-pointer … which he air balled short.

To Barlow's credit, he took another three early in the fourth quarter and drained it. He logged 11 minutes and was quite productive, tallying 12 points on 5-for-6 shooting and four rebounds.

"It felt great," Barlow said of his three. "Got to shoot the ball with confidence. … I've obviously got to get a game feel; I've been missing that. But I worked too hard (in the offseason) to not shoot the ball when I'm open."

Kyle Kuzma hit a three late in the second quarter to build the Bucks' lead to 59-52. After Sixers head coach Nick Nurse's timeout, the team closed the first half on a 8-0 run featuring an Embiid dunk.

The Sixers went just 3 for 16 from long range in the first half, but their low-turnover ways helped mitigate those shooting struggles.

They committed a single turnover in the first half and finished with four giveaways. That's tied for their lowest ever on record in a single game. The Sixers have the NBA's lowest turnover percentage outside of garbage time, according to Cleaning the Glass.

"No matter who you're playing against, teams try to turn you over, they try to speed you up," James said. "Us taking care of the ball, that's a lot of the reason why we won this game."

The Sixers' shooters were bound to start sinking some open looks eventually. Simons, Caldwell-Pope and Edgecombe all made threes late in the third quarter and the team's lead grew as high as 13 points.

Thanks largely to Herro's individuals exploits, the Bucks stayed competitive. AJ Green buried a corner three to cut Milwaukee's deficit to 106-103 with 8:10 to go in the game.

James sought out his shot much more following the Sixers' timeout and did so with great success. He scored four buckets inside over the next four minutes, including a big slam that put the Sixers up 121-112.

It appeared the main questions left were whether Embiid could reach a triple-double and just how many points Herro would rack up.

However, the Bucks forced the Sixers to work down the stretch. Herro got to the 50-point milestone and trimmed the Sixers' lead to two points when he converted a layup with 19.2 seconds left.

The Sixers safely navigated to the final buzzer by the slimmest of margins. Embiid made four late free throws and everyone on the Sixers' sideline was relieved to see that Herro hadn't quite released his jumper in time.

"I try not to complain too much about any win in this league," Nurse said. "The message is we've got to finish a little better."

#2765. The Colts, as expected, won't activate WR Alec Pierce from injured reserve

As the Colts fully embrace the making of business decisions over the pursuit of victories, this one is no surprise.

Via Ian Rapoport of ESPNFL, the Colts won't activate receiver Alec Pierce from injured reserve. He'll miss the rest of the season, with the goal of being fully and completely healthy for 2027.

The situation with Pierce becomes just another one of the tangible examples of the manner in which everything has gone sideways for the Colts over the past calendar year, starting with the November 2025 trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner. Despite knowing that Pierce had an ankle issue that would eventually require surgery, the Colts re-signed Pierce at the outset of free agency to a four-year deal with an annual average of $28.5 million.

While well below the top of the market at the position, it was a major investment in a player with a significant injury. Pierce had surgery in late March and played two games in September (catching five passes for 72 yards) before landing on injured reserve due to an aggravation of the condition.

Given the timing of the deal with Pierce (it was announced just as the March 9 negotiating window opened), it appears that the Colts put a number on the table aimed at keeping him from taking a comparable deal elsewhere. With the Colts promptly trading receiver Michael Pittman Jr. to the Steelers, and in light of the limited production they've gotten from Pierce this year, it's very easy to conclude they should have let Pierce walk, keeping Pittman and moving on.

At this point, with the team at 3-8 and pivoting to quarterback Anthony Richardson Sr., there's no reason to rush Pierce back. From the moment the Colts traded guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner back to the 49ers, the Colts threw in the shoe on 2026. Everything that has happened since then serves only to highlight the fact that they no longer care about 2026 (to the delight of the Jets, who hold Indy's first-round pick next year), and that they're trying to best position themselves for 2027.

Keeping Pierce on IR is just another obvious aspect of that broader plan. And it bolsters the possibility that owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon will decide to give coach Shane Steichen another year.

After a hard-fought Week 7 game at Minnesota saw a potential 3-4 record slip to 2-5, the "we'll get 'em next year" plan was fully activated. While Steichen can be held accountable for the first seven games, it's hard to pin much blame on him for the final ten.

#2763. Aidan Hutchinson wasn't fined for sack that injured Drake Maye

As expected, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson wasn’t fined for the tackle that may have ended Patriots quarterback Drake Maye’s season.

The weekly announcement from the league includes no fines against Hutchinson.

A question emerged as to whether Hutchinson’s sack of Maye amounted to a hip-drop tackle. During the broadcast, Fox rules analyst (and former NFL senior V.P. of officiating) Mike Pereira said it wasn’t a hip-drop tackle. On Monday, NFL in-house rules analyst Walt Anderson confirmed that it wasn’t a hip-drop tackle.

But it’s not Anderson who makes the decisions on fines. Jon Runyan makes those decisions. Not surprisingly, Runyan decided that the tackle was not a violation of the rules.

Under the rules, a hip-drop tackle happens when a player “grabs the runner with one or both hands or wraps the runner with both arms; and . . . unweights himself by swiveling and dropping his hips and/or lower body, landing on and/or trapping the runner’s leg(s) at orbelow the knee.” Anderson said Hutchinson did not “unweight” himself or “swivel.”

Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL in his knee while celebrating the sack. Although it’s not clear whether Maye will play again in 2026, Hutchinson is done for the year.

#2761. James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers

James sees a lot to like — and improve — for East-leading Sixers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James likes to refer to the NBA season as a "marathon."

A few miles in, the Sixers lead the Eastern Conference pack.

With 17 regular-season contests down of 82, the team sits at 14-3, which is 2.5 games ahead of the second-seeded Celtics. The Sixers squeaked out their latest win, a 132-129 decision Saturday over the cellar-dwelling Bucks, but the bottom line is they've become accustomed to finding many routes to victory.

"We want to build habits," James said. "We want to try to take steps forward every game that we get the opportunity. I know sometimes it doesn't happen that way, but we want to do it.

"We want to strive to be as great as we can offensively, defensively and on special teams. A win is a win, but there's ways to win and ways to try to continue to build habits over the course of a marathon."

All sorts of Sixers games have gone down to the wire and they've won every single one.

The team is an incredible 12-0 in clutch situations, defined as games with a point differential of five or under in the final five minutes. The Sixers rank third in the NBA in clutch offensive rating (140.3) and third in clutch net rating (plus-42.0).

"It's good to build that part of our game," James said. "Obviously, we wanted to close the game out a lot better. But a team like that, we know they're going to be scrappy. They're going to play as hard as they can for 48 minutes. … We can learn from that."

James was the centerpiece of the Sixers' fourth-quarter offense Saturday. He scored 13 of his 21 points between the 7:46 and 3:13 mark of the fourth.

The four-time MVP got two buckets on no-nonsense drives and another on an after-timeout isolation hoop over rookie Brayden Burries. James also scored three times on a designed Horns action where he brought the ball up, used Tyrese Maxey's back screen at the elbow and caused serious problems for Milwaukee in the paint.

"We continue to add things to the half-court offense and also to the late-game package," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "That's something we added a few game ago. It's one of those things where, especially if we're in the bonus, we've got some big bodies that can cut down the lane and have feel for timing. It was working. Just keep going to it."

James has grown in comfort with Nurse's coaching style. He knows the Sixers expect him to be a de facto coach on the floor, too.

"I'm just trying to be there for the team in any capacity they want," he said. "Just trying to be an extension of his calls and his commands out there on the floor. Trying to make his life and his job a little bit easier as well.

"But it's been great, not only with him but the whole coaching staff. They've welcomed me with open arms and allowed me to kind of be the voice for the team every day, and take that responsibility."

After a tremendous first impression defensively and some subpar offensive nights, the Sixers' numbers have recently evened out.

The team is 12th in offensive rating outside of garbage time and 12th in defensive rating, per Cleaning the Glass. In essence, the Sixers have been a bit above average on both ends of the floor and downright brilliant in the closing minutes.

It's all added up to an early lead in a very long race.

"I think we've bought into the pass," James said. "We have so many guys that can score the ball at elite levels. … In order for us to be a super-complete team, I think the power of the pass is very infectious. And it's also key for our other guys, to make sure they feel in a rhythm and they feel confident. We've done that from Day 1 and I think it's gotten better and better. … And I think our defense has been really good for the majority of the season.

"(Today) it wasn't so great, but we've been very good defensively throughout the course of the season. … I don't want to say there's anything bad. There's so many things for us to do better for sure. There's games where we can defensive rebound a lot better and there's games where we can not turn the ball over (as much). And there's games where we can be a little more phsyical defensively at the point of attack like (today).

"I wouldn't say anything has been bad, though. That's a good thing. We want to continue to have room for improvement and we don't want to be great in November. That would be weird."

#2759. NFC North continues its historic dominance

The NFC North continues to perform like no other division in the league.

Three of the teams (Lions, Bears, Vikings) have a record of 7-2 through 10 weeks. The Packers are 6-4.

#2758. 4 bold predictions for Broncos’ game vs. Raiders

The Denver Broncos (7-2) will be looking for a sixth consecutive win when they host the Las Vegas Raiders (4-6) on Sunday. The Raiders will have rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza set to make his second career start.

For the Broncos, starting safety Talanoa Hufanga will be back in the lineup after missing the last four games with an ankle injury, while the team's other starting safety, Brandon Jones, will also have a chance to return after missing time with a hamstring injury. The Broncos will be coming out of their bye week, encouraged to take on what appears to be a much easier road than the one they traveled over the first half of the season.

Vance Joseph should be willing to throw the kitchen sink at the rookie in this game and it will be a long day for the QB as the Broncos sack him five times, with one of those leading to a strip sack and fumble recovery, while also creating two interceptions.

Much has been made of the Broncos having to win in one-score games too often, but this week they won't need to. This is a mismatch in many areas and the Broncos are just the better football team. They're at home, they're coming off a bye and they are healthy. Those factors point to a big win.

#2755. Knee surgery complicates Puka Nacua's future

On Friday, Rams coach Sean McVay said receiver Puka Nacua will miss “a couple months.” Nacua is reportedly expected to miss a couple months more than that.

Via ESPN, the recovery time following surgery to repair the MCL tear is four to five months. If accurate, that ends Nacua’s 2026 season.

The problem becomes 2027. Nacua is in the last year of his rookie contract. He hasn’t gotten a second deal, due in large part to the off-field issues that recently resulted in a three-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy and that culminated in an offseason stay at an in-patient holistic rehab facility after he was “drowning myself” in alcohol.

Based on the ESPN report, Nacua won’t be back to 100 percent before free agency starts. The Rams will have to decide whether to sign him to a new deal, to apply the franchise tag (or the transition tag), or to let him become a free agent.

The injury makes it very difficult for Nacua to land in the Jaxon Smith-Njigba ballpark ($42.15 million per year), even though Nacua’s skills and abilities justify that type of deal.

The situation becomes a prime example of the extent to which off-field issues can complicate a player’s financial interests. Without the New Year’s Eve incident that resulted in a lawsuit and, eventually, a diversion program and, inevitably, a suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy, Nacua would have had his second contract by now. Or, at a minimum, he would have had greater standing to hold out (or hold in) until he got paid what he deserves.

Instead, Nacua continued to carry the injury risk into the final year of his rookie contract. And the injury risk became reality 13 days ago, when McVay dialed up a running play to Nacua on third and 11 while trying to run out the clock in a 20-13 game against the Commanders.

It’s a win for the Rams, who may be able to keep Nacua for a lot less than it would cost to give him a market-level contract. However the Rams play the situation, Nacua’s knee injury will make it easier, and cheaper, to re-sign him.

Ultimately, Nacua may have to prove in 2027 that he is back to full strength. And he may have to get through a full season unscathed to unlock the long-term deal his performances earned — but his off-field complications squandered.

Given the way he plays, it’s hardly a given that Nacua will emerge from the 2027 season with the kind of performance, and health, that will finally get him the contract he should have gotten by now.

#2753. The 76ers are fun again, so it's the return of Roob's 76ers Stats!

The 76ers are fun again, so it's the return of Roob's 76ers Stats! originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

This 76ers team is a heck of a lot of fun to watch and fun basketball means fun stats!

At 13-3, the 76ers are exactly a month into the 5th-best start in franchise history and best since they were 14-2 in 2000-01. Which turned out to be a pretty good year. They were 15-1 in 1949-50 and 1966-67 and 14-2 in 1981-82.

To help everybody get through this interminable two-day gap between 76ers games, here's our first 2026-27 installment of Roob's 76ers Stats, with a tip of the hat to Stathead.

→ The 76ers have been out-rebounded by 34 through 16 games (719-685) and their 13-3 record matches the best in NBA history by a team that's been out-rebounded after 16 games. Three other teams have been 13-3 despite getting out-rebounded, most recently the 2013-14 Miami Heat. The others are the 1979-80 Bucks and 2012-2013 Spurs. The 76ers are an NBA-best 6-3 this year when they've been out-rebounded (which means they're 7-0 when they have a rebounding edge).

→ In the win over Orlando Thursday, V.J. Edgecombe had 24 points, eight rebounds, six assists and two steals, and Joel Embiid had 26 points, six rebounds, seven assists and two steals. It was the first time two 76ers had at least 24 points, six rebounds and assists and two steals in a game in 53 years. In a win over the Celtics at the Spectrum in 1973, Fred Carter had 31 points, six rebounds, six assists and seven steals and George McGinniss had 28 points, 16 rebounds, eight assists and three steals.

→ Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, a career 37 percent shooter from 3, is shooting 44 percent so far. Anfernee Simons, a career 38 percent shooter from 3, is shooting 41 percent. Jabari Walker, a career 33 percent 3-point shooter, is at 42 percent. Dean Wade, a career 37 percent shooter, is at 41 percent. Jaylen Brown, a career 36 percent shooter from range, is at 39 percent. The 76ers are shooting just 36 percent as a team from the stripe because James and Embiid have been so bad, but everybody else is off to career-best starts from 3-point range.

→ The 76ers are 7-1 on the road, equalling their best road record ever after eight games. They were also 7-1 in 1980-81, 1981-82 and 1982-83. The 1981 team had the best road start in franchise history, going 12-1 before losing its second road game.

→ With 15.7 points, 6.8 assists and 6.8 rebounds per game, LeBron James is only the fifth 76er ever to average at least 15 ½ points and 6 ½ assists and rebounds through 16 games. The others are some familiar names: Wilt Chamberlain in 1967, Charles Barkley in 1987, Ben Simmons in 2018 and James Harden in 2023.

→ The 76ers already have more wins this year after trailing by 10 points through the first quarter than all but two full seasons since 1950. They had four in 1985-86 and again in 2022-23. The Hawks also have three wins this year when trailing by double digits after the first quarter, but they're 3-4 and the 76ers are 3-2. So they actually have a winning record when they're down by double digits going into the second quarter.

→ With Jaylen Brown (22.6, 6.6), Joel Embiid (20.0, 8.3), LeBron James (15.7, 6.8) and V.J. Edgecombe (13.6, 6.5), the 76ers are the only NBA team with four players averaging 6 ½ rebounds and 13 points. The last time they had four players in a season who averaged 13 points and 6 ½ rebounds was 1961-62 when they were the Syracuse Nationals, with Dave Gambee (16.7, 7.9), Hal Greer (22.8, 7.4), Red Kerr (16.3, 14.7), Dolph Schayes (14.7, 7.8) and Lee Shaffer (16.9, 6.8).

→ Edgecombe's 6.5 rebounds per game are 2nd-most among shooting guards behind only the Grizzlies' Cedric Coward, who is at 8.5. Edgecombe's 6.5 is also 2nd-highest ever by a 76ers shooting guard behind only Greer's 7.4 during that 1961-62 season. Edgecombe averaged 5.6 rebounds as a rookie and his 5.8 career average is highest by a shooting guard who spent more than one year with the 76ers. Greer is second at 5.3. Among all NBA players who've played at least 90 games, Edgecombe's 5.8 average is 11th-highest all-time among shooting guards (although Stathead includes some swing guard-forwards in their data).

→ Joel Embiid's 14.6 shooting percentage from 3 is worst in NBA history after 16 games (minimum 40 attempts). Embiid is 6-for-41 from the stripe this year. The previous 3-point shooting low 16 games into a season belonged to Cedric Ceballos of the Lakers in 1995-96 and the 76ers' Evan Turner in 2013-14. Both were 6-for-43 for 16.3 percent.

#2752. Five sports clubs at Florida State you should know about

Every week, Florida State club sports athletes are sailing on the lakefront, climbing at a local rock gym, or scuba diving in Florida's springs. They're part of the 50 sport and recreation-focused student organizations in FSU's Sport Club Program. Most students know about basketball, baseball, soccer and volleyball, but the other 46 clubs rarely get the spotlight. Here are five more worth knowing.

On Tuesday and Thursday afternoons, the FSU lakefront fills with sailboats with two sailors on each boat. Club Sailing at FSU sails 420s, which have one sailor steering and another controlling the smaller sail in the front of the boat, the jib. The competitive nature of the sailing club demands more than what most expect.

"I don't think people understand the time commitment," FSU biological sciences major Erinne Fenton said in an interview with the FSView. "A lot of people misjudge sailing and think it's a chill hobby where you don't have to do too much, but in racing it's more competitive and you have to spend a lot of time and effort to be good."

There is a sailing club team, which consists of students who enjoyed one of the "learn-to-sail" events at the lakefront and would like to continue their sailing adventures. The competitive team, on the other hand, traveled weekly to regattas across Florida and South Carolina from September to October 2026.

"Sailing wrapped up their season at the Women's and Co-ed fall fleet racing championships," competitive sailing team captain Peter Foley said in an interview with the FSView. "Women's finished 7th overall and co-ed finished 9th with a standout 3rd place finish in A division."

Several FSU students spend their afternoons and weekends catching black bass or other game fish using a rod, reel, line, and lures. The Bass Fishing Club at FSU competes in the Bassmaster College Series and Major League Fishing Abu Garcia College Fishing circuits, rivaling schools across the country.

"Our goal is to build one of the premier collegiate bass fishing programs in the Southeast, and we want the FSU community to know that fishing is a real competitive sport here," Bass Fishing Club President Lucas Saraiva said in an interview with the FSView. "Beyond the college circuits, we host in-club tournaments, give back through lake cleanups, and bring anglers of every experience level together through social events and a shared love for the sport."

The club recognized Florida State alumnus Drew Cook, a professional angler and finished 3rd place in the Bassmaster Elite Series Angler of the Year standings.

He was also named the 2019 Bassmaster Rookie of the Year, earned a Century Belt in 2022, and has achieved multiple Bassmaster Classic appearances and top finishes.

Every Tuesday and Thursday evening, you can catch members of the Climbing Club at FSU at Alchemy Climbing, a rock gym in Tallahassee. They've climbed both in and out-of-state, in Tennessee, and in Alabama.

"Climbing Club at FSU is a great way for students to get out of their comfort zone, try new things, and connect with nature through camping and outdoor climbing trips," junior information, communication, and technology major Aidan Logvinov said in an interview with the FSView. "Whether you're new to the sport and trying it for the first time in the gym, or you're an experienced climber looking for a community, Climbing Club at FSU has something for everyone."

The climbing club plans three to four climbing trips every semester, and there also participate in competitions hosted by USA Climbing. In these competitions, climbers can compete in boulder, speed, or lead climbing. Lead or boulder climbing begins with a redpoint/qualifier format where climbers have a set window of two to three hours to complete multiple routes, followed by an on-sight final, while speed climbing is head-to-head or timed runs on a standard wall.

The FSU Jiu-Jitsu Club teaches Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, a martial art built on grappling and self-defense. Members train three times a week and often team up with other student groups, from Greek life to Reserve Officers' Training Corps.

The club's goal is to foster a welcoming and supportive community where students can challenge themselves, build confidence, and form meaningful friendships. In an interview with the FSView, Jiu Jitsu Club President Nico De La Cadena said he doesn't want anyone to feel intimidated by the idea of trying martial arts.

"Despite the intimidating reputation martial arts can sometimes have, some of the kindest, most humble, and most supportive people I've met have been through Jiu-Jitsu," President of the Jiu Jitsu club, Nico De La Cadena said in an interview with the FSView. "Ultimately, we want students to know that regardless of their experience or athletic background, there is a place for them in our club."

SCUBA at FSU is an official affiliate of the FSU Campus Recreation Sport Club Program, active in the local diving community for over 60 years. This club also isn't just for those that are ready immediately to get scuba certified. Those without certifications can snorkel, swim, or just join the club when they're at a diving site.

The club offers an open water diver course, which costs $350 for students and $400 for non-students and includes equipment, course packets, and state park dive fees. This club has had dives across Florida in rivers and springs like Troy Springs, Vortex Spring, Morrison Springs, Blue Grotto, Fanning Springs, and Rainbow River.

"Our club provides a space for FSU students who are either SCUBA certified or interested in getting certified to connect and dive with each other," social media coordinator for the SCUBA club, Jen Scheckowitz, said in an interview with the FSView. "The most common misconception about our club is that you have to hold a scuba certification to be a part of it."

Kayra Serpenguzel is a Senior Staff Writer for the FSView & Florida Flambeau, the student-run, independent online news service for the FSU community. Email our staff at contact@fsview.com.

#2748. Colts reportedly shutting down WR Alec Pierce for remainder of 2026 season

The Indianapolis Colts are reportedly shutting down wide receiver Alec Pierce for the remainder of the 2026 season, prioritizing his long-term health as the organization prepares for another rebuilding period, according to ESPN's Ian Rapoport.

Pierce has been sidelined since aggravating a left heel injury during Indianapolis' Week 2 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, the same heel he underwent surgery on during the offseason. The 26-year-old receiver missed nearly all of training camp before returning to practice in late August, only to suffer another setback shortly after the regular season began. He has been on injured reserve since September, with head coach Shane Steichen repeatedly declining to provide a definitive timetable for his return.

According to Rapoport, Pierce has been working extensively throughout his rehabilitation and had been pushing to return for the final few games of the season. However, the Colts are reportedly unwilling to risk another setback, instead focusing on having him fully healthy for the beginning of the 2027 campaign. While Pierce had hoped to return before the end of the year, the organization's decision effectively brings his disappointing 2026 season to an end after just two appearances.

The news comes during what has become an increasingly difficult season for Indianapolis, which has fallen to 3-8 following Thursday's loss to the Houston Texans. With the Colts already having traded several established veterans, including wide receivers Keenan Allen and Josh Downs, the organization has little incentive to rush one of its most important offensive players back onto the field during a season that is unlikely to produce a playoff appearance.

Pierce signed a four-year, $114 million extension during the offseason following a breakout 2025 campaign in which he recorded 47 receptions for 1,003 yards and six touchdowns, leading the NFL in yards per reception for the second consecutive season. Expectations were understandably high entering 2026, with Pierce expected to become one of the central pieces of Indianapolis' offense. Instead, he finishes the season with just five receptions for 72 yards, a frustrating outcome for a player who had established himself as one of the league's most dangerous vertical threats.

His absence also leaves the Colts with an extremely inexperienced receiving corps over the remainder of the season. Laquon Treadwell, Ashton Dulin, Anthony Gould, Nick Westbrook-Ikhine and rookie Deion Burks are among the remaining options, placing additional pressure on the younger players to contribute as Indianapolis evaluates its roster for the future. With Anthony Richardson now back under center following the release of Daniel Jones, having Pierce available would have provided a much-needed downfield threat, although protecting his long-term health is clearly the more important consideration.

From Indianapolis' perspective, the decision makes plenty of sense. With significant changes expected during the offseason and a new general manager set to take over, ensuring Pierce returns fully healthy should be a much greater priority than attempting to squeeze a few additional games out of him during an increasingly disappointing season.

After an injury-plagued year that never truly got started, the Colts will now hope that a full offseason of recovery allows Pierce to return to the level that earned him one of the NFL's largest wide receiver contracts.
